paragraphs.source_en: I thought to myself, "If this is the extent of it, then rehearsing the lines together will surely produce some absurd spectacle!" I looked up at my master, only to find that he appeared quite serious. My master asked again, "Then, besides you, what sort of people took part in the reading?" "All sorts of people. The courtesan was played by Mr. K, a bachelor of law; with his mustache, his simpering delivery of a woman's lines was really amusing. And the courtesan has a scene where she suffers a fit of stomach pain, so..." "Even in a reading, must one act out a stomach-pain attack?" my master asked, looking somewhat worried. "Yes, because expression is terribly important." Mr. Tofu kept assuming the air of an artist through and through. "Did the stomach-pain attack go smoothly?" my master asked, with a brief flash of wit. "The first stomach-pain attack was a little less than ideal." Mr. Tofu answered with a witty line of his own. My master asked, "And what role did you take?" "I was the boatman." "Well now, you were the boatman?" From my master's tone, it sounded as if he were saying, "If you can manage the boatman, then I could at least manage the brothel clerk." My master then stated, with no attempt at politeness, "Your boatman was not very successful, was it?" Mr. Tofu showed no sign of displeasure, but replied in the same calm tone, "It was because of that boatman that our otherwise enjoyable gathering last time ended so anticlimactically. As it happened, four or five schoolgirls were lodging next door to our hall; somehow they had heard that a reading was being held that day, and they came to the window to listen. I was using the boatman's assumed voice and had just begun to get into the spirit of it, thinking that all was going well and reading on triumphantly... perhaps my expressions were too extravagant, for the schoolgirls who had been holding back their laughter suddenly burst out laughing all at once. I was certainly startled, and certainly embarrassed; the reading that had been going so well was snapped in two, and I simply could not pick it up again, so we had no choice but to break up the meeting there." If that was what Mr. Tofu called a successful first reading, then imagining what a failed one would be like was enough to make one laugh. Before I knew it, a rumbling sound came from my throat, and my master stroked my head all the more gently. To be cherished for laughing at people was, of course, something to be grateful for, yet it also made me feel a little uneasy. "That was most unfortunate." In the middle of the New Year season, my master actually uttered a condolence-like phrase. The visitor said, "From the second meeting onward, I intend to redouble our efforts and make it more splendid. My coming here today is entirely for that purpose: I should like you too, sir, to join us and lend us your full support." "I could never act out one of those stomach-pain attacks!" My master, negative in all things, immediately began to decline. "No, no.

paragraphs.source_en: There is no need for you to suffer a stomach-pain attack; this is the register of supporting members..." he said, and solemnly took a small notebook from a purple silk wrapping cloth. "I should like you to sign here and affix your seal." So saying, he opened the notebook and placed it before my master. When I looked, I saw the names of a whole company of presently renowned doctors and bachelors of literature, written there in neat order. My master said, "Well, I do not mind becoming a supporter. But what obligations are there?" It seemed that my master, who feared putting himself forward like an oyster, was somewhat uneasy. The visitor said, "As for obligations, there is really nothing in particular we must ask you to do; it will be quite enough if you simply write down your name and thereby show your approval." "In that case, I shall join." As soon as my master heard that no duties were required, he at once became lighthearted. His look seemed to say, "So long as there is no responsibility, I would even sign my name to a covenant of rebellion." Moreover, to have even his own name enrolled among the names of so many celebrated scholars was naturally the highest honor for my master, who had never before experienced such a thing; so it was no wonder he agreed so readily. "Excuse me a moment, please." Saying this, my master rose and went into the study to fetch his seal, dropping me from his lap onto the floor with a thud. Mr. Tofu picked up a piece of cake and stuffed it into his mouth at one bite, then mumbled and struggled with it there for quite some time. This reminded me of my own rice-cake affair that morning. By the time my master returned from the study with his seal, the cake in Mr. Tofu's stomach had more or less settled down. My master seemed not to notice that one piece of cake was missing from the plate; if he had noticed, the first one to be suspected would certainly have been me.
